* **EN 301 549**: A European standard for accessibility requirements for ICT products and services.
* **WCAG 2.2**: The latest Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, which define how to make web content more accessible to people with disabilities.

articles.title: April Zhu on Taste, Judgment, and Designing with AI
articles.description: Singapore-based product designer April Zhu, trained in architecture and creator of the Colorfigures and Tinycharts AI skills, explains how she designs with AI. She left slow-moving architecture for tech's faster feedback loops, grew Colorfigures from a hand-drawn washing machine, and won't outsource her taste and judgment.
articles.one-liner: Designer April Zhu argues that while AI can handle production and brainstorming, the core of design lies in human taste and judgment.

summary.what: Product designer April Zhu shares her transition from architecture to tech, emphasizing that AI is a tool for output, but human-led evaluation is required to distinguish quality from 'vibe-coded' mediocrity.
summary.why: Designers are increasingly struggling with the devaluation of manual skill; this reflects a shift where the 'designer' role is moving toward curator and editor rather than primary creator.

articles.deep-summary:
* Focus on using AI to brainstorm large volumes of variations rather than relying on it to make final creative decisions.
* Maintain a clear distinction between the tool used (AI, Figma, Photoshop) and the output, which should be judged solely on human taste.
* Designers are increasingly shifting toward 'AI-native' workflows that bypass traditional heavy tooling like Photoshop.
* Future UX will likely move toward dynamic, personalized interfaces rather than static design systems.
* Professionals should remain wary of the 'hedonistic treadmill' where increased productivity leads to more work rather than more leisure.
articles.decoder:
* **Vibe-coding**: A dismissive term for AI-generated code or design that 'feels' correct at a surface level but lacks underlying structural quality or intentionality.
* **Third place**: Social environments separate from the two primary environments of home and work, such as parks, libraries, or cafes, which are essential for community spontaneity.

articles.title: Why Enterprise Dashboards Fail Even When They're Well Designed
articles.description: Enterprise dashboards can fail despite excellent visual design because adoption depends on organizational trust, shared definitions, and established workflows rather than charts alone. When different departments interpret the same metrics differently, even accurate dashboards become unreliable, while competing priorities and requests for additional features can undermine their usefulness. Establishing governed metric definitions, involving stakeholders in decisions, and addressing the social dynamics surrounding data can improve adoption more effectively than repeatedly refining visual layouts.
articles.one-liner: Enterprise dashboards frequently fail because they address design aesthetics while ignoring the underlying organizational trust and data governance issues.

summary.what: The article argues that dashboard adoption is a social and organizational challenge; success requires unified metric definitions and stakeholder buy-in rather than visual polish.
summary.why: Visual flair often masks data chaos; until organizations agree on the 'source of truth' for metrics, even a perfectly designed dashboard will be ignored or misused.
summary.takeaway: Before redesigning a dashboard, audit your organization's metric definitions and stakeholder trust; if definitions are contested, focus on governance, not UI.

articles.title: Working with designers
articles.description: Designers can transform functional but ordinary interfaces into significantly better experiences, bringing a different perspective from the technical and planning-oriented culture common among engineers and product managers.
articles.one-liner: Designers provide an essential perspective different from engineering-heavy teams, but having more than one designer at a time frequently creates friction.

summary.what: Sean Goedecke argues that designers offer unique value because they are not 'people of the spreadsheet' like engineers and PMs. He notes that multiple designers often clash over subjective aesthetic choices, making the development process inefficient. He also notes that while design systems are difficult to maintain across fragmented technology stacks, they remain the only viable way to scale consistent UIs.
summary.why: This illustrates the inherent tension between the technical requirement for consistent, repeatable component libraries and the subjective, creative nature of design.

articles.deep-summary:
* Designers are culturally distinct from engineers and PMs, which is a structural advantage.
* Multiple designers on a single project often leads to circular feedback and redundant effort.
* Design systems suffer from a 'principal-agent' conflict: the owners prioritize beauty, while the users prioritize shipping functional requirements.
* Cross-version compatibility (e.g., using a React design system in an HTML/CSS app) remains a major, persistent engineering tax.
* Software doesn't always require 'design' in an aesthetic sense; many functional systems are successful despite poor user experience.
articles.decoder:
* **Design System**: A collection of reusable components, standards, and documentation that provides a framework for building consistent user interfaces.
* **Air cover**: Organizational support from management to shield a team from external pressure or scope creep.

articles.title: What Makes Icons Feel Professional
articles.description: Consistency alone does not make icons feel professional - a clear point of view, restraint, careful finishing, and a growing library do.
articles.one-liner: Professional-grade icon sets succeed through deliberate restraint and a consistent conceptual point of view, rather than just technical alignment.

summary.what: The Streamline team details that high-quality icon sets are defined by a specific 'point of view' (e.g., brutalist vs. soft), the intentional removal of non-essential detail, and rigorous peer review. They highlight the importance of library depth, where having a deep, growing, and comprehensive collection prevents teams from using inconsistent 'workaround' icons.
summary.why: Professional design assets are increasingly judged not by their individual complexity, but by their ability to remain invisible and consistent within a broader, evolving design system.

articles.deep-summary:
* Consistency is a baseline requirement, not the differentiator for professional quality.
* A 'point of view' guides decision-making before technical grids are even applied.
* Excessive detail creates noise; professional icons keep only what makes them recognizable at a glance.
* 'Finished' icons require refinement of small details—such as curves and spacing—that a basic consistency check might miss.
* A reliable library must provide variants and specific actions to prevent 'workaround' drift.

articles.title: UX Trends for 2027: Seven Shifts Shaping the Future of UX Design
articles.description: Seven shifts will shape UX design in 2027, including agentic interfaces, generative UI, and AI agents as users.
articles.one-liner: UX design is shifting toward agentic interfaces and generative UI as AI becomes both the designer and the primary user of digital products.

summary.what: The UX Design Institute identifies seven trends for 2027, primarily centered on the impact of AI: the rise of agentic interfaces (interfaces that perform tasks), generative UI (on-the-fly component creation), and designing for 'AI users' that interact with software via APIs rather than visual elements.
summary.why: The shift toward agentic interfaces means software is moving away from static 'point-and-click' flows toward intent-based interactions, fundamentally changing how developers structure frontend backends.

articles.deep-summary:
* Interfaces will move from static layouts to adaptive, generative experiences that respond to user intent.
* Designers must begin accounting for non-human users (AI agents) as a primary interface target.
* Agentic design prioritizes outcomes over navigation, often reducing the need for traditional page-based flows.
* Personalization will shift from simple user data to deep context-aware interfaces generated by LLMs.
* Ethical design will evolve to include transparency regarding whether a user is interacting with a human or an automated system.
articles.decoder:
* **Agentic interface**: A UI designed for an AI system capable of executing complex, multi-step actions on a user's behalf.
* **Generative UI**: User interfaces that are dynamically constructed or adjusted in real-time based on context and user input, rather than being hard-coded by developers.
